summary: Gives guidelines for designing new application protocols that work well through NATs. Many protocols break when addresses are rewritten, so designers should avoid embedding addresses and similar pitfalls. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT box rewrites the addresses in the packets that pass through it, and a protocol that also mentions addresses inside the data it sends breaks as a result. This memo is the list of things to avoid and to do when writing a protocol that has to work through such a box. The main rule is simple: keep the addresses in the packet headers, and do not repeat them inside the data.

subtitle: Advice for protocol designers on building applications that survive address translation without special help.

tldr.problem: A NAT rewrites the addresses in the packets on the way out, and many protocols carry addresses in their payload as well, so they break when they cross one.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives application designers a list of things to avoid and to do: do not put addresses or port numbers in the payload, use names instead of addresses, keep to one connection, let the client open every connection, do not rely on the address mapping staying the same, and avoid fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: The advice is aimed at the most widely deployed form, NAPT, and the memo notes that end-to-end IPsec does not work across a translator while TLS does. It is Informational.

today: RFC 3235 is an Informational memo giving design guidance for application protocols, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It is advice rather than a specification, and it was written when NAT in homes and small offices was becoming the common case. The terminology and protocol issues it refers to are in RFC 2663 and RFC 3022.

sections.title: Why the Guidelines Exist
sections.content:
Other documents describe Network Address Translation: the Terminology and Considerations document, the Protocol Issues documents, and the implications of NAT for the Internet architecture. The focus of this memo is to give recommendations to authors of new protocols about the effects to consider when designing them, so that special handling is not required at NAT gateway points.

When a protocol is unable to pass cleanly through a NAT, the use of an Application Level Gateway may still permit the protocol to operate. Depending on the encoding used, such a gateway may be difficult or easy to construct, and in some cases it may not be possible at all. While adjunct to NAT, the formulation of protocols that cannot directly operate through NAT should be considered such that the gateway design may be simple and automated. These gateways typically operate inside small routers along with the NAT component, and ideally should be simple and not require excessive computation or state storage.

Many of the same issues in application design that create problems for NAT also create problems for firewalls. An application designer would do well to keep this in mind, because any protocol that requires special handling by NAT or firewall products will be more difficult to deploy than one that requires no special handling.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the memo is to spare every router vendor from writing another special case. A protocol that needs special handling at a NAT needs the same handling in every product, and that is what makes deployment slow.

sections.title: Basic NAT, NAPT and the Other Forms
sections.content:
Network Address Translation presents a challenge to some existing applications. The proliferation of NAT, especially in homes and small offices, cannot be dismissed: the marketing of these technologies to homes and small businesses is often focused on a single-computer environment, so providers give out a single IP address to each user, and NAT has become a popular choice for connecting more than a single system per location.

The most common problem associated with NAT implementations is the passing of addressing data between stations, and where possible applications should find alternatives to such schemes. Two common forms of traditional NAT exist. With Basic NAT, only the IP addresses of packets are altered, and many applications will operate correctly with it. With Network Address Port Translation, both the IP addresses and the source and destination ports for TCP and UDP are potentially altered by the gateway, so applications passing only port number information will work with Basic NAT but not with NAPT. Application designers should strive for compatibility with NAPT, because this is the most widely deployed form and the one most likely to see the greatest penetration in homes and small offices. Not all applications lend themselves to the architectural model that NAPT imposes.

The other forms come later in the memo. Bi-directional NAT makes use of DNS mapping of names to point sessions originating outside the private realm to servers inside it, with lookups performed by a DNS application level gateway, and addresses are mapped one to one. Unlike traditional NAT devices, these are amenable to peer-to-peer applications. Twice NAT is address translation where both source and destination addresses are modified because of addressing conflicts between two private realms, and it also maps addresses one to one. Multi-homed NAT uses multiple NAT implementations to provide redundancy, sharing configuration information so that sessions might continue through a fail-over; unless the multiple implementations share the same external addresses, sessions will have to restart regardless. Realm Specific IP is a different approach altogether: clients inside a private realm that use it are aware of the boundary between private and public, and access a server to allocate address and optionally port information, so the packets they create need not be altered on their way out. That technique can permit IPsec to function, but it assumes there are only two realms, and with several levels of NAT the advantages are wasted.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two everyday kinds. One rewrites addresses only. The other rewrites addresses and port numbers, and it is the one almost every home router does. The rule of thumb that follows from that is simple: write for the harder one.

sections.title: Issues Affecting Every Kind of Translator
sections.content:
Peer-to-peer applications are problematic in a NAT world, while client-server applications are more generally workable. Peer-to-peer applications rely on each peer being reachable as a server, bound to a listening port and able to accept connections for the other to connect to. With NAPT there are likely to be many machines behind one address. Some NAT implementations can be made to work for UDP-based peer-to-peer applications, depending on how the UDP sessions are tracked: if the device tracks the tuple of private address, private port and public port, then an outbound UDP packet can establish a channel through which traffic can arrive from a source other than the one originally contacted, because the source IP address is not used to match incoming packets to UDP sessions. Devices that track source and destination addresses in addition to port numbers will not permit third-party packets, and because NAT is often implemented alongside stateful inspection firewall functionality, that is the more secure behaviour.

End-to-end IPsec will not work in the presence of a NAT implementation, and application designers may want to explore TLS as a transport mode that will traverse NAT cleanly.

Applications should use fully qualified domain names rather than IP addresses when referring to IP endpoints, because private addresses must not be allowed to leak to the other endpoint. The HTTP and HTML protocols show how this can happen today: a page can be specified with a numeric address, for example http://192.168.1.10/index.html, which would likely create a problem if that address is on a server behind a NAT gateway, because users outside the gateway would not be able to reach it. Duplicate addresses between realms make it worse: a link with a private address embedded in it may resolve to a completely different system on the reader's own network, and sessions involving several translators are especially vulnerable to address reuse of this kind.

Not all NAT devices implement multicast routing protocols, so designers should verify that the devices in the networks where their applications will run can process multicast traffic.

With the exception of statically configured bindings, applications should not assume the address mapping will be maintained from one session to another. RSVP is the example given: it forms one connection to reserve resources and then starts the actual session, and the two sessions do not necessarily overlap, so there is no guarantee the NAT will keep the binding. Applications that rely on later sessions being mapped to the same host address may not function without a gateway. It is also entirely possible to have several levels of NAT between the two endpoints, and the lifetime of the mapping at each level has to be considered. Load balancers and similar devices may map a single address and port to several real endpoints, so a mapping to one actual system may not survive across such intermediate boxes.

Finally, do not assume systems know their own IP addresses. A system behind a NAT may be reachable through a particular address that it does not recognize itself, and with static one-to-one mapping a server has an address from the private realm and may not know the public address that maps to it. Some such systems may not know their own DNS names, while others may.
sections.plainLanguage: The problems that hit every kind of translator come from one thing: the address a host sees on the far side is not the address it has at home. So do not put addresses in the data, refer to hosts by name, and do not assume the address you were given last time will be given again.

sections.title: Recommendations for NAPT
sections.content:
Most of the NAPT-specific issues are grouped here, because NAPT is the most common form of NAT in routers, especially in smaller offices and home offices.

Avoid the use of IP address and port number information in the payload of packets. While in some cases an application level gateway will let such protocols work, that presupposes every NAT device can be updated in a timely fashion to support a new protocol, which is unlikely. It is also important to avoid assuming that address and port pairs are unique beyond the scope of the present session, because load balancing devices implementing NAT may map later sessions to other systems in the private realm.

Independent sessions, such as those used by POP or SMTP, are preferred to protocols that manage a bundle of related sessions, such as FTP. The term session here means any association between end systems over any transport protocol or combination of protocols. In FTP, port information is passed over one TCP connection and used to construct a second connection for the data. Using a separate connection makes the end of the file easy to determine, though other schemes could use a single connection. HTTP, for example, uses a header and content length approach, and has evolved to allow multiple objects on one connection, cutting the connection establishment overhead. A new file transfer function could be built that does most of what FTP does without the extra connection. The goal is to keep to single connections where possible, since that keeps addressing information from having to cross the network, though multiplexing traffic over a single connection can create problems as well.

Origination of connections is also important. Where possible the client should originate all connections. FTP is the most obvious example, where by default the server opens the data connection to a port on the client, the client having specified that port with a PORT command over the control session. The passive open option in FTP, PASV, remedies this, since the client opens the connection itself. With client-opened connections the standard functions of NAPT process the request as they would any other simple TCP connection, so an application level gateway is not required. Where session bundles are unavoidable, each session in the bundle should originate from the same end station.

The choice of transport protocol matters too, because NAPT gateways must track which sessions are alive and flush old ones. TCP has clear advantages, with specific beginning and end of session indicators in the SYN and FIN packets. For UDP there is no clean way to know when an end station has finished using a session, so implementations use timeouts to guess, and if an application does not send data for a long period the translation may time out. NAT implementations also use timers for TCP sessions, since the FIN packets may never come, for example if both end stations die. Implementers often provide several timeouts, one for live TCP sessions, one for TCP sessions on which a FIN has been seen and one for UDP sessions, and it is best when such flexibility is provided, although some implementations apply a single timer to all traffic. Protocols other than TCP and UDP can work with traditional NAT in many cases, provided they do not carry addressing information, but for NAPT the use of any other protocol will be problematic unless those protocols are programmed into the implementation. It is also worth noting that NAPT deployments are based on the assumption of a client-server application model, with the clients in the private realm.

Applications should also attempt to avoid fragmentation when packets pass over NAPT devices. If two stations in the private realm pick matching fragmentation identifiers and talk to the same remote host, it may be impossible to tell which fragments belong to which session. A clever implementation could track fragmentation identifiers and map them into a unique space, though it is not clear how many do so. Ideally applications should limit packet size, use Path MTU Discovery or both, although at least some firewall and NAT devices block Path MTU Discovery, apparently believing all ICMP packets are evil. Some implementations reassemble fragments before forwarding and many do not, so designers are advised to assume that the devices do not reassemble.
sections.plainLanguage: For the common case the advice is concrete: keep the address out of the data, use one connection, let the client open it, stick to TCP, and do not fragment. FTP's passive mode is the model, because the client opens the second connection and the router never has to be told a port number.

sections.title: Performance Implications
sections.content:
Resource utilization on the NAT gateway should be considered. An application that opens and closes many TCP connections will use more resources on the router than one that performs all its transfers over a single connection. HTTP 1.0 opened a connection for each object on a page, whereas HTTP 1.1 permits the session to be held open for additional objects, and the latter imposes a lower overhead because the gateway is maintaining state on one connection rather than several.

New session establishment will typically remain a software function even in implementations where the packet-by-packet translation work is handled by hardware forwarding engines. High-performance NAT boxes may be built, but protocols that open many sessions instead of multiplexing will be slower than those that do not. Applications with different types of data, such as interactive conferencing, require separate streams for each type, and the protocol needs of each stream must be optimized; while the goal of multiplexing over a single session is preferred, there are cases where that is impractical.

The latency of the translation overhead is implementation dependent. On a per-packet basis, for established sessions, only the source or destination IP address is replaced, the source or destination port for NAPT, and the checksums for IP and for TCP or UDP are recalculated. The functionality can be implemented efficiently in hardware or in software.
sections.plainLanguage: Every connection the gateway carries costs it memory and processing. A protocol that opens a connection per file or per object makes the router work much harder than one that keeps a connection open and reuses it, so the design choice is a performance choice as well as a compatibility one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Network Address Translators have implications for IPsec, as noted above. When application developers are considering whether their applications function with NAT implementations, care should be given to the selection of the security methodology. TLS operates across translation boundaries, while end-to-end IPsec will prove problematic in many cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose the security method with the translator in mind. TLS works because it protects the payload and does not care about the addresses underneath. IPsec protects the whole packet, so it cannot survive the addresses being rewritten.

items.title: Peer-to-peer is hard
items.text: Each peer has to be reachable, and behind NAPT many machines share one address.

items.title: End-to-end IPsec fails
items.text: IPsec does not work across a translator; TLS does.

items.title: Use names, not addresses
items.text: Referring to endpoints by domain name avoids leaking private addresses.

items.title: Do not assume the mapping lasts
items.text: The address a session gets may differ from the one the next session gets.

items.title: Multicast may not be routed
items.text: Not every NAT device handles multicast traffic.

items.title: Systems may not know their own address
items.text: A host behind a NAT may not recognize the address it is reachable at.

items.title: Keep addresses out of the payload
items.text: The address and port belong in the packet headers, not in the data.

items.title: Use one connection
items.text: One connection means no addressing information has to cross the network.

items.title: Let the client open it
items.text: The client should originate every connection, as FTP's PASV mode does.

items.title: Prefer TCP
items.text: TCP has clear start and end markers; UDP sessions end only when a timer fires.

items.title: Avoid fragmentation
items.text: Matching fragment identifiers make it impossible to tell fragments apart.

items.title: Watch the path MTU
items.text: Limit packet size or use Path MTU Discovery, since some devices block it.
